# THE CHRONICLE
## *OF THE* WALDENSIANS,

->That is:<-

->*Concerning the origin, teachings, and life, as well as the manifold oppressions and persecutions of the* WALDENSIANS.<-

---

### THE 1st CHAPTER.

->From where the Waldensians obtained their name, the circumstances by which they separated themselves from the Roman Church, where they first lived, and how they were later dispersed.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'O' featuring elaborate floral scrolls and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>

Around the year 1160 after the birth of Christ, there lived in Lyon, France, a wealthy, learned, and godly <term>merchant</term> <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205) was a leader of a lay spiritual movement that eventually became known as the Waldensians.</note> named Peter Waldo; he gave great alms to the poor, and while he shared that physical bread with them, he simultaneously exhorted them that they, above all else, [should seek] Jesus Christ, the true Bread of Heaven, and the

<summary>This is the title page and opening paragraph of a history of the Waldensians, introducing Peter Waldo of Lyon as a pious merchant who provided for both the physical and spiritual needs of the poor in the 12th century.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Peter Waldo's conversion and the beginnings of his spiritual movement in Lyon, following the introduction on page 1 which described him as a wealthy merchant providing for the poor.</meta>

### Chronicle of the

true Food of Souls.

Some recount that *Waldo*, by means of the following tragic event, began to lead a blameless and nearly <term>Apostolic</term> <note>Living in imitation of the simplicity and missionary zeal of Jesus’s original twelve apostles.</note> life.

Once, in the evening after a meal, when he was with several of his good friends and making merry with them, it happened that one of the company died a sudden and unexpected death. They were all greatly terrified by this; but especially *Waldo*, who took this to heart as a visible judgment of God. From that hour on, he dedicated himself to a life of sincere repentance, spending his time reading the <term>Holy Scriptures</term>. He also published several useful and edifying books and taught the poor who were accustomed to receiving alms from him.

In addition to this, he was moved to the diligent reading of the Holy Scriptures and to consider the state of religious affairs more deeply, not only because of the great blasphemies that had become common among the <term>Clergy</term> <note>The body of ordained ministers and priests in the Church.</note>, but also due to the terrible <term>Idolatry</term> <note>The author is referring here to the worship of images or religious objects, which the Waldensians rejected.</note> that rose higher and higher. It reached such a point that anyone was condemned to death who could not believe that, at the word of the priest, the Body of our Lord *Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Jesu Christi"</note>—essentially, as long and as broad as He hung upon the Cross—was present in the small

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the account of Peter Waldo’s opposition to the Roman Catholic Church in Lyon, specifically addressing his rejection of transubstantiation and his eventual exile following a papal decree.</meta>

->### WALDENSIANS<-

<meta>sig: A 2</meta>
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

round <term>Host</term> <note>The wafer used in the sacrament of the Eucharist.</note> was: where one also had to worship the aforementioned Host, falling down before it in the streets and holding it to be a God.

Against such false teaching and ungodly life, *Waldo* took a stand, and seriously rebuked many other abuses of the Roman Church.

The Archbishop of Lyon could not tolerate this; he therefore forbade him from teaching, as he was a <term>layman</term> <note>A member of the church who is not a member of the clergy.</note>, and threatened that if he continued, he would be treated as a <term>heretic</term> <note>Someone holding beliefs that contradict established church doctrine.</note>.

But *Waldo* did not allow himself to be deterred by this, but answered: He could not remain silent in such a weighty matter concerning the salvation of mankind; he must obey God—who commanded him to speak—more than men <note>Waldo is echoing the biblical response of the Apostles in Acts 5:29.</note>.

Upon this, the Bishop wanted to have him arrested; but he could not bring it about, since *Waldo* was greatly beloved by everyone and had remained hidden in Lyon for four or five years with the help of his good friends.

Thereafter, when **Pope Alexander III** became concerned that his prestige and high authority over all churches might be endangered, and that *Waldo* might draw a larger following to himself, he commanded the Archbishop there to proceed against *Waldo* and his followers as against heretics and to completely root them out; thus, *Waldo* and his fellow believers were driven out of Lyon.

# Chronicle of the

But **Waldo** went into the <term>Dauphiné</term> <note>A historical province in southeastern France.</note> and into the mountains of **Provence**, on the borders of **Piedmont**, and even into **Piedmont** itself, where the Churches then quickly increased in number.

He also traveled into **Picardy**, where he taught with great success and gained many companions in the Faith. But since they could not remain safe there for long, many of them moved from there to **Germany**. These believers spread out into **Bohemia** (to which **Waldo** himself also traveled with some and where he spent the remainder of his life), into **Bulgaria**, **Croatia**, **Dalmatia**, **Hungary**, and many other places.

### C H A P T E R  I I I.

#### Concerning the teachings, life, and church ministers of the ancient Waldensians.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'W' featuring floral or leafy motifs within a rectangular frame, spanning three lines of text.</image-desc>
What the ancient Waldensians taught and believed is known from the *History* which **Jean Paul Perrin** <note>Jean Paul Perrin was a 17th-century historian from Lyon whose work "Histoire des Vaudois" (1618) is a primary source for Waldensian history.</note> of Lyon published openly. In his third book, he printed the following pieces of the ancient Waldensians: namely, the instruction of children; the explanation of the **Ten Commandments**; of the **Christian Apostolic Faith** <note>The Apostles' Creed.</note>; of the Holy **Our Father** <note>The Lord's Prayer.</note>; the teaching of the **Sacraments**; of the **married state**; of the visiting of the sick; and of the confession of sins.
   We shall here only present their ancient **Confession of Faith**, just as the same is to be found in the aforementioned writer on page 79; and it reads as follows:
   I. We believe, and hold as firm, all that which is contained in the twelve Articles of the **Apostolic Faith**; and we hold everything that does not agree with these Articles to be **heresy**.

### W A L D E N S I A N S.

...are just as well situated for the reading of the Holy Scripture as the Preacher.

Regarding their Teachers, they were for a long time called **Barbes**, that is, Fathers, so that in **dangerous** <note>original: "periculose," from the Latin *periculosus*.</note> times they might not be discovered and brought into trouble; they were generally learned and well-practiced in the arts, languages, and Holy Scripture, as well as in the teachings of the early Church, as can be seen from their remaining writings.

They were especially diligent and industrious, both in the instruction of their students in the fear of God and in works of brotherly love; principally, they applied great diligence and performed great labor in copying the Books of the Holy Scripture for the benefit of their students before printing presses emerged:

For just as they themselves were excellently practiced in these (which resulted from the fact that no one was admitted to the Holy Preaching-office who had not learned by heart the entire Gospel of **Matthew**, the Gospel of **John**, all the Epistles of the Apostles, and a large part of the writings of **Solomon**, **David**, and the Prophets), so they also earnestly commanded the reading of the same to their listeners with such benefit that the monk **Reynerius** <note>Reinerius Saccho, a 13th-century inquisitor and former member of a similar group, who wrote detailed accounts of the Waldensians.</note> and others like him were forced to admit that they had seen some among the common people of the Waldensians who were so learned they could recite entire Books of the Holy Scripture from memory, word for word.

# Chronicle of the

Alongside the **Preaching-Ministry**, they also practiced their **Handicraft** <term>Handt-werck: a manual trade or craft, such as carpentry or weaving, practiced to ensure self-sufficiency.</term>: many devoted themselves to the practice of **Medicine** or the **Healing Arts**, in which they were very famous; with this, they were on the one hand helpful to their listeners in times of need, and on the other hand, were able to provide for their necessary livelihood during their frequent travels.

Their **Preaching**, **Child-instruction**, and other **Godly exercises** were similar to the current practices of the **Reformed churches**.

They held a general assembly of the Preachers every year, particularly in the month of **Autumn**; at these meetings, those who wished to enter the **Preaching-Ministry** were examined. There, those were also ordained who would visit the distant congregations in **Calabria**, **Apulia**, **Sicily**, and other places; there they usually had to remain for two years, until others were sent in their place by another **Synod** <note>A formal council or assembly of church leaders.</note>.

**Claude de Seyssel**, Archbishop of **Turin**, in a Treatise that he wrote against them, gives this testimony regarding the <term>Waldensians</term>: that they are upright in their life and conduct, and are found to be irreproachable, of whom no one had cause to complain, as they have applied themselves with all their might to live according to the commandments of God.

# Chronicle of the

...they had themselves baptized after the manner of the early church; that they taught the Articles of the Christian Faith and the commandments of God.

When the King learned of this through those he had sent, he swore and said: that the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval Christian movement that emphasized apostolic poverty and the authority of the Bible, often facing persecution for rejecting Roman Catholic doctrines.</note> were more pious than he and his people.

And when the King heard at the same time that in **Dauphiné** <note>original: "Delphinat"; a historical province in southeastern France.</note>, and especially in the **Valley of Freissinière** <note>original: "Dal Fraissiniere"; a remote alpine valley that served as a refuge for religious dissidents.</note>, under the **Archbishopric of Embrun** <note>original: "Ambrum"</note>, a people lived who, like wild animals, lived without religion and considered the **Roman Churches** to be evil; he likewise sent his Confessor and the <term>Official</term> <note>A judge or administrative officer of an ecclesiastical court.</note> of **Orléans** there to investigate the state of the matter.

When these envoys arrived at the aforementioned places, they examined those people concerning their faith and life.

But the Archbishop of **Embrun**, hoping to enrich himself through the confiscated goods <note>It was common practice for the property of condemned heretics to be seized and divided between the church and the state.</note>, earnestly urged the envoys that they should hastily condemn these people as Heretics, and allow their goods to pass to him as the Archbishop of that land. ->### WALDENSIANS.<-

[Merin]dol, **Cabrière**, and other nearby places had been subjected to such great oppression and suffering: he therefore ordered an investigation concerning their Faith and Life, and commanded **Sir William du Bellay**, his Lieutenant in **Piedmont**, to diligently research everything.

The same sent two honorable men to **Provence** <note>original: "Provancen"</note> and had them investigate how the <term>Waldensians</term> <note>A medieval Christian movement that sought to follow apostolic poverty and rejected several Roman Catholic doctrines; they were frequently targeted by the Inquisition.</note> conducted themselves in matters of faith and life, and in what manner the <term>Parliament</term> <note>The Parlement of Aix, which was the regional high court responsible for the increasingly harsh decrees against religious dissidents in Provence.</note> behaved toward them.

They found that the Waldensians were industrious and God-fearing people, who had come from **Piedmont** to **Provence** about two hundred years earlier, and had received uncultivated lands or fields as fiefs. Since that time, they had supported themselves honestly and harmed no one. They were peaceable and neighborly, paying their debts without any legal compulsion, and showing all kindness to strangers. The people in **Provence** also testified that one could recognize the Waldensians among all others by their godly conduct; for no one heard them curse, name the **Devil**, or swear in vain. Furthermore, they did not associate with people who spoke indecently or cursed.

See, in this way, many from the opposing party spoke of the Waldensians themselves.

Let us now also look for a moment at what those who later adopted and confessed a similar faith judged regarding them.

In the beginning, the Monks had all the power to seize and persecute the faithful according to their wish and will. They used to gather the people by the ringing of alarm bells <note>Original: "klocken-storm," the practice of ringing church bells in a specific rhythmic pattern to summon a mob or the community for an emergency or public execution.</note>, whenever and wherever they wished.

And where they had the slightest suspicion, neither father nor mother, nor friend, nor neighbor dared to speak against them.

If anyone had given a Waldensian (to speak of the best case) a glass of water or a handful of straw in the prison, they were immediately executed as an evildoer.

When someone was suspected on account of the teaching of the Waldensians, neither *Notary* nor *Advocate* dared to serve him: and such persecution extended not only during the person’s life, but also continued after death: For they also raged against the bones in the graves, for they were dug up and cast into the fire <note>Posthumous trials and executions of remains were a common practice of the Inquisition to justify the confiscation of an estate from the deceased's heirs.</note>.

The heirs dared not take up any matters of the estate, but had to remain silent and renounce all things.

And so that the Monks might keep the poor people in all places all the better in fear and awe

# WALDENSIANS

In order to maintain their power, they were accustomed to parade their prisoners, leading them in their cloister-walks and processions as if in a triumph; they dressed them in red cassocks <note>A long, loose garment or cloak</note> adorned with yellow crosses, as a sign that they had been condemned for the sake of heresy.

Some were forced to walk about in their shirts, barefoot and bareheaded, carrying a burning torch and wearing a noose around their neck. They had to stand before the church doors but were not permitted to look inside, especially when the Host <note>The consecrated bread used in the Eucharist</note> was being elevated, as a sign that they were not worthy to behold it or to partake in it.

Some were sent across the sea to the Holy Land, others elsewhere; meanwhile, the monks took possession of their property. Even when they eventually returned home, they did not dare to ask how it had fared with their goods, wives, or children.

And how great and terrible the persecution was can be gathered from this: when it was asked whether those who had held the Holy Supper <note>The Protestant term for the Eucharist or Communion</note> with the Waldensians, or had otherwise had any fellowship with them, were to be excused, the monks' answer was that they were not to be excused, since they could not plead ignorance.

For the Waldensians had already been publicly executed and killed for a long time and in many places with great effort and labor, in such a way that from now on no one needed to doubt whether they had been treated rightly or wrongly.

# Chronicle of the

The crafty schemes and cunning of the monks can also be recognized from this: namely, that they refused to dispute matters of faith with any Waldensian <note>A member of a medieval pre-Protestant movement that emphasized poverty and the authority of the Bible</note> in front of the common people. This was out of fear that they might be convicted of their own errors by the Waldensians using the Holy Scripture.

And even if someone had wished to renounce their faith, they still would not have granted him his life, unless he betrayed all others present and his own fellow believers. They did not allow anyone to come to a public defense. They did not promise to save the life of anyone before the people who had been publicly condemned to death.

They said that one must proceed and carry on with them in such a manner that the deed is always held as confessed, and only the circumstances are inquired after, such as: "How many times have you heard the preaching among the heretics <note>original: "Ketters"</note>, and joined in their prayers? In what place did you harbor and shelter the heretics?" etc.

The monks were also accustomed, when they examined the believers, to look into a book every time, as if they already had everything on paper about which they were examining and questioning them.

They also used to threaten the prisoners immediately with death, saying: "Prepare yourself, and renounce your error, for you must die; and you may bear yourself patiently in all that shall befall you." They did not let

A short time after the year 1205, Pope *Innocent* <note>Pope Innocent III</note> wished, for the second time, to completely root out the *Waldenses* <note>A medieval Christian movement often persecuted as heretical by the Roman Catholic Church.</note>; at first with sweetness, through the preaching of certain Monks: thereafter with violence, through fire, sword, and open wars.

The Monks could accomplish nothing with preaching, for they were unlearned: on the contrary, the *Waldenses* were well-versed in the Holy Scripture and led a godly life; but the Roman Priests lived in open blasphemies and gave great offense.

The *Waldenses* sent word to the Bishops that their Teachers were willing and ready to openly defend their doctrine from God's word, and desired that a gathering might be held to speak with one another concerning *Religion* <note>original: "Religie"</note>.

The Bishops and Monks were satisfied: they summoned one another to *Montreal* <note>original: "Mont-Reael"</note>, near *Carcassonne*, in the year after *Christ's* birth 1206; and there, Arbitrators <term>Scheyts-Heeren: neutral judges or mediators appointed to oversee a formal debate</term> were appointed by both parties: two Bishops and two *Albigensian* <note>A term often used interchangeably with Waldenses or Cathars in this context to describe the local dissenters.</note> Preachers.

# CHRONICLE OF THE

There was dispute especially concerning the **Mass** <note>The central act of worship in the Catholic Church, which the Waldenses often critiqued</note>, but one of the Bishops with his Monks were so cornered <note>intellectually defeated in debate</note> that they all, being at a loss, departed from there with shame and wished to dispute no longer.

The Monk **Peter of Castelnau** <note>original: "Petrus van Chasteauneuf," a papal legate whose assassination triggered the crusade</note> caused a Nobleman, near **Nîmes**, so much grief and trouble that he <insert>the nobleman</insert> slew him.

The Pope wished to blame this homicide on **Count Raymond of Toulouse**; for this reason, in the Year 1208 at the **Lateran**, he caused a **Bull** <term>Bulla: a formal decree or public letter issued by a Pope</term> to be sent out, in which he placed the Count under the **Ban** <note>Excommunication and loss of legal protections</note>; and to all who wished to march against him, he promised indulgence <note>remission of temporal punishment</note> for all their sins: Admonishing also that these heretics, the **Waldenses**, must be persecuted and rooted out much more earnestly than the **Saracens** <note>A medieval term for Muslims; the Pope was prioritizing this internal crusade over the Crusades in the Holy Land</note>, and that their lands should be taken from them and given to the **Catholics** to possess.

Count Raymond offered his excuses, saying that he had not slain the Monk; that he who had done such a thing had fled to **Beaucaire** to his friends, and that violence and injustice were being done to him; especially since his enemies had charged him with such things, etc. But all these excuses were in vain: For the Pope’s army began to fall upon his land in the Year 1209.

In this Army of the Pope were found many Counts and **Prelates** <note>High-ranking clergy such as bishops or abbots</note> with the people under their command, to all of whom the Pope promised **Paradise**. If Count Raymond now wished to keep his land, he had to consent to everything that the **Papal Legate** (who had brought this people with him) proposed to him.

When Montfort had conquered the fortress of Minerve <note>original: "Menerben"</note>, situated on the Spanish border, a certain Abbot there delivered a sermon to the citizens, intending to bring them back to the Roman Church; but their unanimous answer was:
> We will not leave our faith, but we reject your faith of Rome: you labor in vain; for neither death nor life shall turn us away from our faith.

Because of this, the Legate and the Lord of Montfort were troubled; they had a great fire lit and burned 140 persons, women as well as men, and these all went joyfully into the fire.

After this, Montfort besieged the city of Lavaur <note>original: "La Vaur"</note> for six months, which he also caused to be scaled and stormed: and having been taken, everyone was hewn down, except for 80 noblemen, whom the Lord of Montfort caused to be hanged.

# Chronicle of the

In the year of Christ 1210, twenty-four Waldenses <note>Followers of a proto-Protestant movement founded by Peter Waldo</note> were captured within Paris, of whom some were walled up between two walls <note>A form of execution or life imprisonment where the victim is immured</note> and the others were burned.

In the year 1211, the aforementioned Legate <note>The Pope's official representative</note> passed away, and that very suddenly and unexpectedly; a certain Tedese <note>Theodosius, a papal notary</note> came in his place.

This Legate enticed Count Raymond to him with smooth words, saying: He wished to settle his affairs; but when he came to him, the Legate placed him under the Ban <note>Excommunication from the Church</note> anew, not because of the murder—for he had been falsely accused of that—but because he had not rooted out the Albigenses according to his promise.

The Count retreated to Toulouse <note>original: "Colosa," likely a variation of Tolosa</note>. The Bishop, because the Count was under the Ban, did not wish to tolerate him there in the city; over this, the Count became so enraged that he commanded the Bishop, together with the entire Clergy <note>original: "Cleresy"</note>, to vacate the city upon pain of death, which they then did.

The Bishop sought to avenge himself, gathered people together, and marched with Montfort <note>Simon de Montfort</note> before the city; but they were received several times by the sallying forces in such a manner that they had to retreat and were forced to seek better air <note>A contemporary idiom for fleeing a dangerous or pestilential situation</note>.

The Legate marched forward with a portion of the people, fell upon a strong tower, and had one hundred Albigenses burned alive.

At that time, the King of England <note>King John "Lackland," who was Count Raymond's brother-in-law</note> came to the aid of the Albigenses.

# W A L D E N S E S.

In the year 1212, in January, the King of Aragon wrote to the Council which was being held at Lavaur <note>original: "Vaur," a stronghold of the Albigenses</note>, and pleaded for the Count of Toulouse <note>original: "Tolosa"</note>, his son and council, as well as for other Lords and Counts; but all was in vain and to no purpose. For the Council answered him by a letter on the 16th of January, 1212, boasting of many and great mercies which had been shown to the aforementioned Lords—and especially to the one of Toulouse <note>original: "Cholosa"</note>—by the Pope and his Legate; and that notwithstanding this, they had persisted in their abominable heresies, and for that reason, to their great shame, they were now excommunicated and placed under the Ban.

When the King of Aragon now wished to submit to the Pope’s tyranny, and treated of this at Toulouse with Count Raymond and the one of Comminges, the Count of Foix <note>original: "Foir"</note> also traveled there, and dissuaded them with very earnest and brave words from that which they had intended. By this, the King was moved to compassion, took up arms, and sent to the one of Montfort <note>Simon de Montfort</note>, that tyrannical persecutor of the <term>Waldenses</term> <note>A medieval spiritual movement declared heretical by the Catholic Church</note>, a <term>Letter of Defiance</term> <note>original: "Assegh-Brief," a formal declaration of hostilities or a challenge</note>.

Upon this, the one of Montfort sent to various places in Europe, and had the Crusade preached by the Bishops and Monks; for they no longer had to deal only with a Count of Toulouse, Foix, Comminges, etc., but with a mighty King, who had become the head of the <term>Albigenses</term> <note>A dualist religious sect in Southern France targeted by the Church</note>: and if one did not come to his aid, then it would...

# Chronicle of the

The battle near Toulouse soon begins again. A soldier says to those of Montfort that he should be on his guard, for the enemy is sallying out from the city. Then Montfort spoke—who at that same time was in the Mass—saying he wished first to see his Savior <note>A reference to the elevation of the Host during the Catholic liturgy</note>; and if the priest had not shortened the Mass, he would have been slain at the altar.

Montfort sits upon his horse; the horse itself was shot in the head and runs off with such turbulence that Montfort could not hold it back. A soldier from the city became aware of this and shoots him through a leg; immediately thereafter comes a large stone from an engine <note>original: "geschut," referring here to a trebuchet or stone-throwing catapult</note> which a woman had fired, and it took his head entirely away, on the day after Saint John the Baptist, 1218.

Count Raymond <note>Raymond VI of Toulouse, the primary opponent of the Crusade</note> defeats the enemy and thanks God for the victory.

In the year 1219, the Legate <note>The papal representative overseeing the Crusade</note> writes to the King in France, exhorting him that he should march toward Toulouse with all his might and avenge the death of the Count of Montfort. He promised him that he would bring it to pass that the Pope would have the Cross preached throughout the whole world <note>A formal call for a new Crusade, where participants wore a cross as a symbol of their vow</note> to obtain help.

But shortly thereafter the Pope dies, and the Legate travels to Rome, saying: he could no longer carry out such work on account of his old age.

In the year 1220, on the 6th of August, the monk Dominic <note>Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican Order</note> also died, who through his Inquisition and preaching against the Albigensians had become very rich.

Pope Gregory IX persecuted the Waldenses to the utmost: his Legate <note>A high-ranking papal representative</note> had their houses torn down and drove them out of all Italy; he also sent two Dominican Monks <note>original: "Predicker Monnicken"; the Order of Preachers, who led the Inquisition</note> to Milan, so that they might investigate and destroy everything.

In the year 1229, a Council was held at Toulouse to implement the Inquisition; there it was decided in seven Articles as follows: We forbid all laypeople the possession of the books of the Old and New Testaments, and forbid explicitly that anyone shall have such in the common tongue <note>The vernacular language of the people, rather than Latin</note>.

Around the year 1230, the Waldenses in Germany were cruelly persecuted by a monk named Eckard; who thereafter, being struck in his conscience, was converted and burned at Heidelberg for the true Religion.

At this very time, Conrad of Marburg was made an Inquisitor by the Pope; he persecuted the Believers quite terribly and tested, with glowing irons <note>The "ordeal by fire," a medieval judicial practice</note>, whether they were good Christians.

In the year 1234, when the Count of Toulouse and the Count of Foix were dead, it appeared as if it were entirely over for the Albigenses.

But Trencavel, the Bastard of Béziers, took up the cause of the Albigenses with force, whereby the Pope's Legate and the Bishop of Toulouse were strongly opposed; and he of Béziers held the field until the year 1242, and did the enemy great damage.

# Chronicle of the

When, in the year 1243, the Count of Toulouse <note>Raymond VII, who had been forced to submit to the French crown and the Church</note> had already paid the imposed sum of money—which we mentioned previously—and had arrived back in his own land, there was great lamentation everywhere concerning the Inquisition and the tyranny of the monks. This reached such a point that, not long thereafter, nine monks were slain by the common people. Thereupon, Pope Innocent <insert>IV</insert> came to Lyon and thundered with his Ban <note>An official decree of excommunication and outlawry</note> against those who had killed the monks. The Count of Toulouse had to pay the price for this when he petitioned the Pope for a dispensation and permission to marry his niece <note>original: "Bas"</note>, the daughter of the Count of Provence. He was also refused permission to bury his father’s remains in a consecrated place, as his father had died while under the Ban.

In the year 1250, the Inquisition against the Believers was undertaken with ever-increasing severity; these measures were confirmed and approved by Pope Alexander IV, by Clement IV in the year 1264, and by John XXII <note>The text says John XXII, though the date 1276 suggests John XXI; the author likely refers to the ongoing papal succession supporting the Inquisition</note> in the year 1276.

And wherever one of them could be apprehended, he was executed without mercy.

In **Provence**, one named **Albertus de Capitaneis** <note>Albert Cataneo, a notorious inquisitor</note> allowed himself to be used boldly in the persecution of the **Waldenses**.

The **Archbishop** continues with his tyranny against the Believers; and because they could not afford the costs to go to law with him, they fled out of the country—except for one named **Jacob Poliveri**, who protested against such unjust proceedings and demanded a copy of everything that had been undertaken against him. # CHRONICLE OF THE

For the Believers <note>The Waldenses, a pre-Reformation Christian movement</note> conducted themselves so manfully—with God’s help—that the enemies were defeated everywhere, but especially in the Valley of *Angrogne*.

For as soon as the Believers noticed the enemies' intentions, they occupied the passes and guarded them well. They took long wooden shields that covered a whole man and held the passes; behind them stood the Archers with bows and crossbows <note>original: "arm-rustingen"; refers to mechanical bows or armor-piercing weaponry</note>. # WALDENSIANS.

# WALDENSIANS.

Pope Alexander VI <note>Rodrigo Borgia, reigned 1492–1503</note>; but others said that one could accomplish such things with less expense through the Legate, the Cardinal of Saint-Sixtus <note>original: "Sanct Xist"</note>, who was residing in France.

When they had now obtained two special Bulls <term>Bulls: formal proclamations issued by the Pope, named after the lead seal or 'bulla' attached to them</term>, in which indulgence <note>A grant by the Pope of remission of the temporal punishment in purgatory still due for sins after absolution</note> was given for Simony <term>Simony: the buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or offices</term>, Theft, Murder, Usury, Fornication, Adultery, Sorcery, Sacrilege <note>original: "Kercken-roverye," literally church-robbery</note>, Perjury, and all kinds of cunning and deceit, public robbery, and apostasy from the faith; yet the Archbishop would not agree to it, but said: one could buy such things from the Pope for money, whose Court was nothing other than a marketplace and a house of profit; and thus he wished to give nothing back to anyone, even though the Indulgence was most abundantly shared with them.

In the year 1506, under King Louis XII, at the instigation of the Prelates and Monks, the Waldensians in Provence were vehemently persecuted.

But although men have attempted to suppress them in all places and to root them out entirely; yet trustworthy Histories testify that around the year 1530, eight hundred thousand Waldensians were still found who held fast to the pure doctrine of the Gospel.

Around the year 1532, the Believers in Piedmont began to hold gatherings to preach and to offer their prayers openly, and they feared no one any longer; but committed themselves to the dear God, with such

As soon as the Bishop of Sisteron <note>original: "Cisteron"</note>, the Abbot of Cavaillon, and others learned of this in the year 1534, they had them sought out and brought into the prisons. After Bersur had received this command, he immediately wrote to the officials <term>Amptluyden: local administrative or judicial officers</term> of the above-mentioned Bishops, and earnestly requested them to delay the trials of the imprisoned Piedmontese in their territory until his arrival.

But this writing of his came too late, for thirteen of the prisoners had already been delivered into the hands of the secular authorities <note>This usually meant they were handed over for execution, as the church "relaxed" heretics to the state for punishment</note>.

Meanwhile, Bersur arrived in Provence and learned so much from the prisoners that he obtained a sufficient knowledge of all the Waldensians who resided within the Duke's territory.

# W A L D E N S I A N S.

With this information he returned again to Piedmont and showed everything to the Inquisitors; they themselves persisted with the Duke until he gave the aforementioned Bersur full power to lay hands upon all the Waldensians.

But in order that he might put his instructions into effect all the better and more hastily, he took five hundred men with him, both on horseback and on foot, and fell with violence upon the borders of Angrogna <note>original: "Angrogne," a key Waldensian valley</note> before the people were aware of it, plundering, robbing, and murdering everyone he encountered. The believers, on the other hand, left their plows and other field-work, and fell upon their enemies with their slings with such a brave and undaunted spirit that they struck down a good many of them, wounded many others, and put the rest to flight, chasing them away and reclaiming the loot.

This proceeding went very much to the heart of the Lord President, the Count of Lucerna <note>original: "Lucerne"</note>, and the widow of the Lord of Angrogna: they wrote an earnest letter of reproach to the aforementioned Bersur regarding this matter, stating that he had thus attacked their subjects without their knowledge, and warned him at the same time not to undertake such a thing again.

What sort of answer followed this writing is not mentioned. # WALDENSES.

If we allowed our Pastors <note>original: "Zielzorgers" - literally 'soul-carers', the spiritual leaders of the community</note> to be taken from us, we would be following a worldly <note>original: "vleeschelijcken" - literally 'fleshy' or carnal, implying human wisdom rather than divine</note> counsel, upon which a curse hangs. For if our enemies gained this advantage over us—that no one remained to comfort, teach, punish, or exhort us—they would surely apply all their power to ensure that the door remained permanently shut against our Pastors in the future; through whose service we have been so well instructed and strengthened against the temptations of the world.

And since we would be accused of being rebels and disobedient anyway, should we try to recall them later, it is surely better that we keep them now, and not allow ourselves to be robbed of the fruit of their service. It is also better that we be regarded as people who serve God, and who protect those whom God has sent to them to teach and preach to them, etc.

This, and whatever else was said, could nonetheless not prevent the Ministers <note>term: Predicanten - Protestant preachers or pastors</note> from being asked to withdraw for a time and stay nearby in Pragila <note>Pragelato, a neighboring valley then under French control where the Waldensians had many brethren</note> with their fellow believers. But then, one quickly became aware of the judgments of God upon them, and the beginning of all curse and judgment.

There was a great weeping among all the people, and the entire Valley was filled with crying; women and children escorted the Ministers to the summit of the mountain.

They then stormed the Fortress and defeated the opponents, driving away the entire faction of their enemies and killing a great number of them.

At this, Duke Emmanuel Philibert <note>The Duke of Savoy (1528–1580)</note> became greatly incensed and wished to take revenge upon the prisoners; but the Duchess <note>Margaret of France, Duchess of Savoy, who was known to be sympathetic to the Reformers</note> pleaded for them and stilled the Duke's wrath to the best of her ability. For she pointed out to him the manner in which their Deputies, contrary to the promises made, had been treated and mistreated, and that they saw their own destruction before their eyes and could not have acted otherwise.

Despite this, the Duke was so urged and influenced by the Pope's Legates that he forced the Deputies to attend the Mass <note>term: Misse - the central liturgical ritual of the Roman Catholic Church, which the Waldensians rejected</note> and commanded them to publicly ask forgiveness from God, the Pope, and the Church, with the promise that they would, in the future, live according to their commands and institutions. And after this had occurred, he sent them home again and ordered the Fortress to be rebuilt.

# WALDENSIANS.

After this, the Commissioner Corbis issued an order to those in the Lucerna Valley <note>The Val Lucerna, one of the three primary Waldensian valleys in the Cottian Alps</note> that they must attend the Mass and subject themselves to all ordinances of the Roman Church, upon pain of death.

The response of the Reformed was briefly this: Their religion was consistent with the Holy Scripture, the Faith of the Apostles, and the Doctrine of the early Christian Church. If anyone could convict them of any error using the Holy Scripture, they were willing and ready to abandon it. If it could also be proven to them from the Holy Scripture that the Mass and other similar institutions of the Roman Church were holy and good, they would gladly accept <note>original: "aennemem," likely a printer's error for "aennemen"</note> them.

But if this could not be shown to them, they earnestly desired that they might be left in peace and quiet with their religion.

Following this answer, they remained unmolested for several days. But in April of this year, 1560, the Lord of Raconis came to Saint John <note>San Giovanni, a Waldensian parish</note> and made his presence known at a sermon on a Wednesday. After the sermon was finished, he spoke much of the Duke’s <note>Duke Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy</note> leniency and testified that the fact they had been so violently persecuted had not happened with his prior knowledge. Nevertheless, one had to consider the means to pacify His Highness; he therefore asked the believers what they thought would be most useful for this purpose. After they had decided together, in the fear of God, to do nothing at all that might be detrimental to the honor of God or contrary to His Holy Word, they began to exhort all their people with the highest earnestness: that they should, through true repentance and faith, as well as through fervent prayers, take their refuge in God; that they should provide themselves with all necessities, and bring their household goods and the weak persons into safety in the highest reaches of the nearest mountains. When the Count now saw that his designs would not succeed, and that the Reformed <note>The Waldensians, who had formally aligned with the Protestant Reformation</note> had resolved to risk themselves to the last man, he changed his mind and wished to use cunning instead of force. But while still occupied with this, he marched with his people on the fourth of December <note>original: "Wintermaent"</note> against Taillaire and Villar. The party that had marched against Villar sought to climb to the heights in a large village. But when the appointed watch saw them, they—after they had offered their prayer—set themselves against the enemies with such manliness that they killed some of them, wounded others, and put the rest to flight. After this had happened, they came to the aid of those at Taillaire, where the battle lasted a long time and very many of the enemies were slain; but of the believers, not one was killed—only three who were slightly wounded, yet they were very quickly healed again.

The Count wished, so it appeared from the outside, to make peace again; he requested four of the most prominent men of Angrogna to negotiate with them. These men, after their return, said that they had been friendly received by the Count, and that he tes-

98

The violence of the enemies, which was closest to **La Cour** <note>Likely referring to La Torre Pellice, a central town in the Waldensian valleys, or a specific fortified manor known as "the Court."</note>, caused a great terror among the inhabitants of that place. And since they did not dare to openly take up arms, nor seek help from their neighbors (for their envoys were with the **Duke** <term>original: "Hertoch," referring to Emmanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy</term> and were hoping for a merciful answer), they resolved to leave their houses and save their lives. To that end, some retreated to the high mountains into the caves, even though it was the middle of winter; others fled elsewhere. When the **Soldiers** <note>The troops under the command of the Count of la Trinité.</note> learned of this, they plundered everything that was still to be found, and even those hidden on the mountains were not safe from them.

In a certain cave, they found a mother with her daughters; these they wounded unto death. In another cave, they found a man who was one hundred and three years old, together with his granddaughter. They killed the man; they intended to violate the daughter, but she threw herself down from the **rocky cliff** <term>original: "steenrotze"</term> and died.

When the godless soldiers had finished plundering that place, they went into the community of **Villar** <note>Villar Pellice, a village further up the valley from La Torre.</note>. There, they likewise plundered everything, taking men and women away in bonds. These captives were forced to carry the very loot and drive the cattle that had been stolen from them. The poor prisoners were severely mistreated by them: one maddened villain bit off a man's ear, saying he wanted to carry **Heretics'** <term>original: "Ketters," a derogatory term used by the Catholic forces for the Waldensian Protestants</term> flesh into his own country.

They begged them to have mercy on themselves, their wives, and their children, as they and their ancestors had lived in the land for several hundred years and had behaved in such a way that no one could complain about them. the **Viceroy** appeared; for as soon as they had arrived at ***Foscalda*** <note>Modern-day Fuscaldo in Calabria, Italy.</note>, seventy of them were taken prisoner and brought to ***Montalt*** <note>Montalto Uffugo.</note> before the **Inquisitor Pantza** <note>Giulio Panza, a notorious commissioner sent to suppress the Waldensians in Calabria.</note>, who put them all together on the **rack** <term>A torture device consisting of a rectangular frame with rollers at both ends; the victim’s limbs were tied and pulled to induce intense pain and joint dislocation.</term>.

Among others, they had one named ***Steffen Carlijn*** <note>original: "Steffen Carlijn"</note> so hideously tortured that his intestines fell out of his body onto the earth. The Inquisitor intended to force them through such terrible torments to confess to shameful things and to say "yes" to his questions—things they had never thought of in all their lives—only to make them all the more hated among the common people. When the Inquisitors captured beautiful young daughters among the prisoners, they never allowed them to appear in public again; just as at that time nine beautiful young daughters were lost, of whom no news could ever be heard again.

How hideously many were tortured and yet remained steadfast, we shall learn in the sixth Chapter.

After this, the Inquisitors moved to ***S. Agata*** <note>Sant'Agata di Esaro.</note>, where they also delivered a great multitude to the **Secular Authority** <note>The civil government; the Church would "hand over" convicted heretics to the state to carry out the death penalty, as the Church officially avoided shedding blood.</note>.

And if anyone wished to speak a good word on their behalf, they were also immediately put on the rack as someone who desired to defend the **Heretics** <term>Those whose religious beliefs contradicted official Catholic dogma; in this period, heresy was considered a capital crime against both Church and State.</term>, so that no one dared to speak another word.

**Pope Pius IV** sent the **Marquis of Buccianico** <note>original: "March-graef van Butiane"; Giovan Girolamo Castiglione, the military commander tasked with the suppression of the Waldensians in Calabria.</note> with such force to completely **root out** <note>original: "uyt te roepen"; to exterminate or drive out entirely.</note> the Believers, with the promise that his son would receive a **Cardinal’s hat** as an honor if he could cleanse **Calabria** of such people. This was easily done by him, as the **Inquisitors** killed almost everyone they could catch; the strong were sent to **Spain** to serve on the **galleys** <term>Large, oar-powered warships where prisoners were chained to benches and forced to row in brutal conditions, often until death.</term>, while the women and children were sold or strangled.

Now that we have heard at length about the horrific persecutions of the year 1560, we shall now proceed to the following times.

When, in the year 1561, at the beginning of January, those who had been appointed by the Believers and sent to the **Duke** <note>Emanuel Philibert, Duke of Savoy.</note> at **Vercelli** <note>original: "Verceil"</note> arrived back in the **Luserna Valley** <note>original: "Dal Lucerne"; one of the primary Waldensian Valleys in the Piedmont region.</note>, there was hope of hearing good news through them, but in vain: for they brought word that they had not only failed to obtain any concessions, but that even harsher decrees had been issued, namely to force them into the **Roman Religion** <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> or to root them out entirely. Monks and priests had been ordered to come into the Valleys; also, the force intended to be used against them was so great that it would be impossible to resist.

Because of these unexpected tidings, the Believers became deeply distressed: and to this was added that the **Preachers** <note>original: "Predikanten"; the spiritual leaders of the Waldensian communities.</note> in **Piedmont** <note>The region in northwest Italy bordering France.</note>,

### WALDENSIANS. 119

That all who had fled should return again, to possess and inhabit their houses and property, which should be returned and restored to them; namely those which had been taken from them on account of Religion or otherwise in the preceding wars.

That they should be left, sheltered, and protected in all their Liberties and Rights <term>Rights (Gerechtigheden): Specifically, the legal privileges and chartered freedoms granted to the Alpine communities by previous rulers.</term> obtained from His Highness and his illustrious ancestors.

That, where the Mass is held and the Roman Religion practiced in the Valleys, none of them should be required to attend such worship, nor to help promote it.

These and other similar Articles were promised and pledged to the Believers, after they had been most severely persecuted for eight months and attacked with war for seven months.

This peace negotiation greatly displeased the Pope; but the Duke <note>Duke Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy (1528–1580). While initially intent on enforcing Catholic uniformity, he agreed to the peace to stabilize his borders and economy.</note> informed him that such a peace was very necessary for all his subjects.

### Chronicle of the

Those of the Reformed who had been isolated—after they had been overcome with many crafty and deceptive words—signed all of these things.

But all their protesting was in vain; in particular, *Castrocaro*, their greatest enemy, was forced upon them as Governor. And how he behaved toward them can easily be inferred from a few examples of the tyranny he committed.

When he learned that the Countess of *Cardé* and other nobles from lower *Piedmont* had come to *San Giovanni* <note>St. Joan (San Giovanni) was a key town in the Pellice Valley where Waldensian worship was often contested.</note> to receive the Holy Supper <note>The "Holy Supper" refers to the Protestant sacrament of Communion, which was a central point of theological conflict with the Catholic authorities.</note>, he arrived with his soldiers to prevent it.

He commanded the congregation at *Bobbio* <note>The village of Bobbio Pellice, located deep in the alpine valley.</note> to dismiss their preacher because he was a foreigner; and as they were unwilling to do so, he levied a fine against all the Reformed people in *Bobbio*.

Because he bore an exceedingly great hatred toward Lord *Gilles de Gilles* <note>Gilles de Gilles was a prominent Waldensian pastor and leader known for his steadfast resistance to Savoyard encroachment.</note>—as he was the one who had manfully opposed his aforementioned *Articles*—and being unable to drive him out under the pretext that he was a foreigner, he devised other means to dispose of him.

# THE WALDENSIANS.

But when they could not obtain such a confession from him, Joseph Barberi—a great enemy of the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Protestant movement, of which the Waldensians had become a part.</note>—attempted to move him to the Roman Religion <note>The Roman Catholic Church.</note> through many flattering words and promises: and he gave him a Book, in which he, as a sign of his conversion, was to write that he consented to it and believed everything that was written therein.

To this he gave as an answer: he could not do so unless he first knew the contents. Barberi left that book with him for three days, and after the passage of the three days, he demanded an answer from him. Then the Preacher said that the Book was full of errors and blasphemies; he would rather die than approve of such errors and change his religion. Barberi grew very angry at this answer and said: "Bring wood here, lay him upon it, and burn him, without further Trial <term>Trial (Proces): the formal legal proceedings or judicial inquiry which were often bypassed in cases of perceived heresy or political urgency.</term>." To this the Preacher answered: "I am in the hand of God and the judges, and I hope that no violence shall be done to me: and even if one wished to kill me against the law, I submit <note>original: "soo onderwerp"</note>..."

In this year 1565, on the 20th of June, the Duke issued a Mandate <note>A formal decree or law.</note> stating that all those in his land who did not wish to live according to the Roman Religion <note>Roman Catholicism.</note> should declare themselves within ten days and depart from his land within two months.

And since this command was a general one, it was also sent to various congregations, which then caused unspeakable misery and a great multitude of *exulanten* <note>original: "exulanten"</note>, or exiles, of all social ranks and conditions.

Since this persecution was now a general and very severe one, the Believers, alongside earnest prayers to **God**, also took all other good means at hand: they requested the Duchess for her usual intercession, which she, for her part, did not fail to provide in everything that might have served them for the better. But because she could not prevent or turn away all misfortune as she desired, the Believers applied to certain German Princes—and especially to the Elector at Heidelberg and the Elector of Saxony—to seek intercession with his **Highness** <term>Highness (Doorl.): an abbreviation of "Doorluchtigheydt" (Serene Highness), the title of the Duke of Savoy.</term>; who immediately, in the year 1566, sent Lord *Johannes Junius*, a former Councilor of the Electoral Palatinate, to *Turin*.

*Gonzaga*, Duke of *Nevers*, the King of *France's* Governor in the *Marquisate of Saluzzo* <note>An Alpine territory that was a flashpoint of religious and political conflict between France and the Duchy of Savoy.</note>, likewise had everyone he could catch executed and strangled in the year 1567.

Those who fell into the hands of the Archbishop of *Embrun* in *Dauphiné* <note>A province in southeastern France known for its Waldensian populations in the high valleys.</note> were forced to languish in desolate and stinking pits, or die of cold and hunger in the Tower.

So too were the believers in *Piedmont* hunted and banished, and there was no other way to flee but over a high and impassable mountain in the heart of winter, full of ice and snow, over which they might have fled during the night if it had been possible. Because they had with them not only a great number of young and helpless children, but also old and elderly men and women, such a flight was all the more difficult for them.

Likewise, whether he considered those of the Roman Church to be believers or unbelievers.

When the Minister noticed what he intended with these questions, he answered the question with such distinction and so clearly that, even though the Jesuit thought he had not yet been given enough, the most prominent men on his own side admitted it and said: "Father, he has answered you enough, let us go."

After eight days he came again to the same place with new questions, to which he was answered again as the situation required.

And when he came there again after the lapse of eight days, a proper disputation <term>disputation|A formal, public academic or theological debate, usually conducted according to strict logical rules.</term> was organized in the presence of Governor Castrocaro <note>Pantaleon de Castrocaro, the governor of the Piedmont valleys.</note> and a great multitude of people of both religions.

The Jesuit always wanted to run from one question to the other and not stay on one matter, until finally the Governor brought it to the point that one should, at once, [speak] of one matter...

# Chronicle of the

Since from time immemorial our dear ancestors, from father to son, have been instructed in the **Doctrine** and **Religion** which we have known from our childhood, and in which we have instructed our own, in the same manner as we were taught by our elders.

Also, while the **King of France** <note>original: *Vranckrijck*</note> held the **Marquisate of Saluzzo** <note>original: *Marck-graeffschap Saluces*</note>, we were permitted to profess and practice our **Religion** without hindrance or persecution; just as our brothers in the **Valleys of Lucerne**, **Perosa** <note>original: *Peruse*</note>, and others, who—following a special agreement established by our **Sovereign** <term>Landts-Vorst|Refers to the Duke of Savoy, the territorial ruler</term>—have enjoyed the free practice of the **Reformed Religion** <note>The Protestant faith adopted by the Waldensians</note> until this very day.

Nevertheless, his **Highness** <note>The Duke of Savoy</note>, incited more by evil counsel and by passionate people who begrudge us than by his own pleasure and will, intended to burden us, and to 그 end allowed an **Edict** to be issued against us.

By this, it should become known and public to everyone that we are being thus plagued and deprived of our property not for any crime we might have committed against the person of our **Prince**, nor because we have acted in rebellion against his **Edict**.

Acknowledge and make known to everyone that we know and assure ourselves that this **Doctrine and Religion**, which is taught and practiced there in the **Reformed Churches**, as well as in **France**...

### W A L D E N S I A N S.

We humbly pray to that same faithful God of ours, that, just as he holds the hearts of all Kings and Princes in his hand, he may also move the heart of his Highness <note>original: *Doorlucht.*, a formal honorific title for a sovereign ruler</note> to a will of mercy toward those who never offended him, nor ever thought to do so; so that he may find them to be much more loyal and upright in his service than those who incite and drive him to such persecution.

If, on the contrary, it pleases God to leave us in such persecution, then we pray that he would be pleased to arm us with patience and steadfastness, to persevere in the knowledge of the truth until our end, and our descendants after us, Amen.

Following this terrible persecution in the Marquisate <term>March-graefschap|A territory governed by a marquess</term> of Saluzzo, another began in the following year of 1602 in the Valley of Lucerna <note>Now the Val Pellice in the Piedmont region of Italy</note>. For at that time there arrived in Lucerna the Count of Lucerna, Governor Ponte, and Archbishop Broglia, with a large group of monks and Jesuits. All of these took up residence in the Count's palace and summoned all the heads of households <note>original: *Huys-vaders*, literally "house-fathers," representing the family unit</note> who belonged to the Reformed Religion before them. They declared to them that the Duke was not minded to tolerate anyone of the Reformed Religion in the Valley of Lucerna anymore. They were therefore to make a decision: either to attend Mass <term>Misse|The central liturgical service of the Roman Catholic Church</term>, or to abandon everything and depart from the country, never to return. Some suffered a sorrowful fall <note>meaning they converted to Catholicism under pressure</note>; but the majority remained steadfast.

# Chronicle of the

From Lucerna, these Lords traveled to Bibiana <note>original: *Bubiane*, a municipality in the Metropolitan City of Turin</note>, where the majority and most prominent of the people also belonged to the Reformed Religion. There, they disclosed the same command; but not a single person was willing to attend Mass <term>Misse|The central liturgical service of the Roman Catholic Church</term>, for they had all been very earnestly exhorted to steadfastness by several of their leaders.

Consequently, four of the most prominent men were summoned to Turin in the hope that they would show such high honor to the Duke <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy (reigned 1580–1630)</note> that they would agree to attend Mass.

When they arrived there, the first was brought alone before the Duke, who immediately requested that he attend Mass. But he replied that he could not do so without violating his conscience. The Duke said that he desired to be saved just as much as the Reformed; and if he did not consider his own religion—namely, the Roman Catholic Religion—to be the true one, he would not urge anyone else to embrace it. After this, he dismissed the man, who left feeling joyful and comforted; however, he did not dare to reveal what had happened to the others who had been summoned with him.

When the others were then brought before the Duke, they were told that their companion had submitted to the Duke’s will and had promised to change his religion; and that if they did not wish to do the same, they could expect nothing but trouble <note>original: *quaedts*, meaning harm, evil, or misfortune</note>.

-> # W A L D E N S E N. <-

When they were now brought before the Duke, he addressed them in the same manner as he had the previous man. And they gave for their answer: that if they could be left to practice their own Religion, they would consider that a great favor. They confessed their error <note>original: *mis-slag*, a mistake or lapse in judgment</note> and, shortly thereafter, returned once again to the Reformed Church.

Meanwhile, the Archbishop and his monks did not cease their efforts to incite the Reformed in Bibiana <note>original: *Bubiane*</note> and other nearby places to apostasy <term>afval|The abandonment of one's religious faith, in this context, leaving Protestantism for Catholicism</term> through disputations, kind words, and generous promises.

When the Duke <note>Duke Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy.</note>, in the years 1613 and 1614, waged war in Montferrat against the King of Spain, and the **Reformed** also distinguished themselves in that same war with great praise, they encountered people there who spoke of their Religion and said that nothing was more desirable to them than that they might live in the same faith.

But they also found others, especially those who lived in remote, lonely places, to whom strange and miraculous things had been told about the **Waldensians**. It had been said of their soldiers that a regiment would come from the Piedmont Valley, among whom only a few were Christians, while the rest were strange and monstrous people who spoke ill of God, the Virgin Mary, and the deceased Saints. Some of them reportedly had only one eye, right in the middle of the forehead; a fourfold set of teeth with long black fangs; and it was claimed that they roasted their children over the fire and ate them. With many more such strange things, they were accused and made to be hated.

In some places, people both young and old came running to see such strange wonders; in other places, they all fled away from such monsters and trembled before them.

And although the issued Edicts only concerned those who had joined the <term>Reformed Religion</term> <note>The branch of Protestantism following the teachings of John Calvin, which the Waldensians had formally adopted in the 16th century.</note> in the <term>Marquisate of Saluzzo</term> <note>original: "Marck-graeffchap Saluces"; a territory in the Piedmont region of modern-day Italy.</note>, the enemies of the truth nevertheless sought to use them against those who lived in the Valleys of <term>Piedmont</term>. Because the Reformed did not know of this Edict, they attempted to bury one of their dead according to their usual custom in their own churchyard, which was attached to the churchyard of the Papists but was distinguished from it by specific markers. Meanwhile, his relatives <note>original: "bloedt-vrienden"; literally "blood-friends," meaning kinsmen or family relations.</note>, who were many in number, did not cease to petition for his release: whereupon the Duke ordered that his case should be processed without delay; and when it was found that he was innocent, he was released; but on the condition that he would return to **Dronero** <note>original: "Dronier"</note> and engage in further religious debates.

After his release, he returned to the **Val Lucerna**: and when he later wished to return home from a certain journey through **Provence** and **Nice**, he was met on the road by some Papists <note>A term used by Protestants at the time to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> of his acquaintance, who led him with them to **Piedmont** and, out of hatred for his religion, murdered him in a remote place.

In the following year, 1623, the persecution against those who still remained in the **Val de Barcelonnette** <note>original: "Dal Barcellone"; a valley in the French Alps that was then part of the Duchy of Savoy.</note> began violently. A decree was published by which all Reformed believers were commanded either to attend the Mass or to appear in **Turin** before the **Cardinal of Savoy** <note>Cardinal Maurice of Savoy (1593–1657), who was active in efforts to convert the Waldensians.</note>. Although they sought to prevent this persecution through frequent appeals, the aforementioned clergy, through their constant incitement, achieved so much that a new command was issued, by which all were ordered to hear the sermons of the monks under penalty of life and limb <note>original: "lijf- en levens-ſtraffe"; a legal term for capital punishment or severe corporal punishment.</note>: but as they would not do so, they were forced to leave everything and depart. Some then went to **Dauphiné** <note>original: "Delphinat"; a province in southeastern France.</note>, some to **Orange**, others to **Lyon**, and still others went into the valleys of **Piedmont**.

<summary>This page describes the release and subsequent murder of Captain Frans Garnier by his acquaintances, and details the 1623 decree forcing the Reformed inhabitants of the Val de Barcelonnette to choose between Catholicism, legal trial, or exile.</summary>

# CHRONICLE OF THE... 170
<meta>catchword: Dies</meta>

In the year 1624, the Duke <note>Duke Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy (r. 1580–1630).</note> ordered many troops to be recruited: he sent them into **Val Perosa** <note>original: "Dal Peruse"; one of the three principal Waldensian valleys in the Piedmont region.</note>, and commanded the Reformed <note>The Waldensians or members of the Protestant Reformed Church.</note> to demolish six of their churches; and should they refuse to do so, then **Count Taffin** and **Savine**, a nobleman from **Dauphiné** <note>original: "Delphinat"; a province in southeastern France.</note>, would compel them by force with his regiment of Frenchmen. They pleaded earnestly to be left with their churches and freedoms, but it was all in vain.

However, because there were many soldiers among those French troops who were adherents of the Reformed religion, they did not wish to be used against their fellow believers; instead, they requested their discharge, which was granted to them. Nevertheless, some of them remained; when the Evangelicals <note>Protestant believers; in this context, the Waldensians.</note> were attacked, these soldiers joined them and stayed with them until the enemy had once again retreated.

When the aforementioned regiment reached the lower parts and the villages situated on the plains of **San Germano** <note>original: "St. Germain"; San Germano Chisone.</note>, the inhabitants, as they could offer no resistance, abandoned their houses and retreated to the heights, and from there they appealed for help from the neighboring valleys; but the passes were occupied by the enemy in such a manner that assistance could not easily reach them. Furthermore, those of **Val Lucerna** <note>original: "Dal Lucerne"; one of the primary Waldensian valleys.</note> were forbidden, under penalty of life and limb <note>original: "lijf- en levens-straffe"; a legal term for capital punishment or severe corporal punishment.</note>, to provide any assistance to the fugitives; however, even this could not entirely prevent them from doing so.

<summary>In 1624, the Duke of Savoy attempted to force the Reformed inhabitants of Val Perosa to destroy their own churches, leading to a military standoff where French Protestant soldiers refused to fight their own coreligionists.</summary>

### WALDENSIANS.

For this reason, the Count <note>Count Taffin, the commander of the Duke’s forces mentioned on the previous page.</note> traveled to **Lucerna** <note>Val Pellice, also known as the Val di Luserna.</note> and to the Court; he summoned the Ministers, **Syndics** <note>original: "Sindicos"; local magistrates or community leaders.</note>, and other prominent figures of the churches of the **Val Lucerna** to meet. He attempted to persuade them that the army had not moved into the **Val Perosa** <note>original: "Dal Peruse"; a valley where Waldensian and Catholic populations lived in close proximity.</note> for reasons of religion, but only to punish certain rebels. He argued that they should therefore not involve themselves in this business, but rather leave the matter to the Duke.

Whereupon the **Evangelicals** <note>The Waldensian Protestants.</note> pointed out to the Count that this was indeed a war concerning religion, and that for this reason, they could in no way abandon their fellow brothers. At the same time, they pleaded with him to work toward a solution so that this dispute might be settled without further bloodshed.

However, after much dispute, those of the Val Perosa finally decided among themselves to demolish the aforementioned churches, on the condition that the great military force—about ten thousand men strong—would then withdraw; and that once the army had departed, they might rebuild the churches again, according to what had been promised to them.

But while they were busy with the work of tearing down the church tower at **Pinasca** <note>original: "Pinasche"; a village in the Val Perosa.</note>, and settling all disputes with **Lord Sillan**—who had ordered the Reformed inhabitants of **San Germano** <note>original: "St. Germain"; San Germano Chisone.</note> to meet him at **Dubbione** <note>original: "Dublon".</note>—news arrived in great haste that the army had been significantly reinforced and had already launched an attack on San Germano.

# Chronicle of the

When the representatives of the **Reformed** <note>The Waldensian Protestants.</note> heard of these developments, they abandoned the **treaties** <note>original: "Tractaten"; refers here to the ongoing diplomatic negotiations.</note> they had begun and hurried home. There, they discovered that their people had fought against the Enemy for some time during the night, striking down many of them, while not losing a single man on their own side.

**Count Taffin** excused this hasty and unforeseen raid as best he could, and he made a new start with those negotiations with the Reformed that had been set aside. The demolition <note>The destruction of the Waldensian churches, a condition imposed by the Duke's forces.</note> was then recognized and accepted based on the previously mentioned condition, though this was done against the better judgment of many.

Once the churches had been demolished, they requested of the Count that now, according to his promise and the concluded agreement, the army should be led away. But he would not agree to this; [he insisted] that the Reformed must first lay down their arms and level all their erected **ramparts** <term>Schanssen: temporary defensive fortifications made of earth and timber</term>.

But because they perceived the goal he sought—namely, that he might bring that small valley, which includes **St. Germain** and **Pramol** <note>San Germano Chisone and Pramollo, two key Waldensian strongholds.</note>, under his power—they decided to defend themselves in their **trenches** <term>Loop-graven: defensive ditches or entrenchments</term> to the last man. Meanwhile, they did not cease to earnestly request the Count that he would do them no further violence, and that he should not advance further upon them or expose himself: for such a situation would be very regrettable for them <note>The Waldensians are warning the Count that if he advances, they will be forced to fire upon him, despite their desire for peace.</note>.

But all this was little regarded; and some of the Enemy came close to their fortified positions and threw many mocking and abusive words at them: one of the **Reformed** <note>The Waldensian Protestants.</note>, embittered by this, and without the will or approval of the others, shot down a **Captain** <term>Hooftman: a military leader or commander</term> of the Enemy.

### Chronicle of the

...and there received this office of **Prior** <term>Priorschap|The office or rank of a prior, the head of a religious house or monastery</term>, because he promised to propagate the **Popish Religion** <note>original: "Paepsche Religie." A contemporary Protestant term for Roman Catholicism, often used with a derogatory or polemical tone.</note> to the utmost of his ability in the **Valleys**, and in opposition to it, to do damage to the **Reformed**, or, if possible, to abolish them entirely.

And so that he might now fulfill these promises, he resolved to build new monasteries in the **Lucerne Valley** <note>Val Lucerna, one of the core valleys of the Waldensian territory in Piedmont.</note> and to ordain monks to serve in them.

He first persuaded his father to sell his house and other associated buildings at **Cour** to serve as a monastery for the **Franciscan Monks**.

These monks were appointed there in this same year, **1628**, and provided with all necessities in such a manner that they could richly distribute provisions to all the **Papists**, who were still only few in number there.

But they did this not so much for the sake of the **Papists**, to feed them in this time of high prices <note>Refers to the severe famine and scarcity caused by war and crop failure mentioned earlier in the text.</note>, as for the sake of the **Reformed**, to lure them by this means and bring them to apostasy.

But since no one presented or offered themselves because of this, they—and especially the **Prior's mother**—visited all the poor in their houses and exhorted them not to refuse the great alms being distributed by the neighboring monks, but to receive them and turn themselves to the **Catholic Religion**.

But God carried out His work so powerfully among the **Reformed** <note>Members of the Waldensian church who had aligned with the Protestant Reformation.</note> that they resolved among themselves to leave everything behind and move to another place. Because they were unable to sell their houses and goods, they took with them whatever they could and traveled to their fellow believers in the **Lucerna Valley** <note>original: "Dal Lucerne"; today known as Val Pellice, the historical heart of the Waldensian communities in the Piedmontese Alps.</note>, where they were kindly received.

One of them was released by means of a large sum of money, and the other was thrown onto the **Galley** <note>A form of penal servitude where prisoners were forced to row large warships; a common and often fatal punishment for "heretics."</note>, where he eventually died, having valiantly overcome all enticements to **apostasy** <note>original: "afval"; the act of renouncing one's religious faith.</note>. Therefore, he was resolved to remain in his true and **only-saving religion** <note>A common 17th-century theological phrase expressing total conviction in one's faith.</note> until death.

That they testify before the Most High God, alongside their Pastor, that they desire to live and to die in obedience to His Royal Majesty.

That it was also known that the Monks have bound themselves to the rule established in the **Council of Constance** <note>A 15th-century church council. To the Waldensians, it was infamous for the decree that "faith need not be kept with heretics," meaning promises made to them were not legally binding.</note>, namely: that no faith shall be kept with Heretics.

How far the Inquisitors at **Turin** overstep can be seen from their ordinances, which they had printed on April 14 in the year 1643: in which they demand that all Heretics (for so they call the honest people who live in the Valleys) must obtain permission from them to stay in Turin; through which they usurp the office of the Magistrate and overturn the Liberty given to us, who live in the Valleys, namely, to travel freely and safely to Turin.

Then the Monks, in all silence, took possession of that house and did not cease to be a burden to the Reformed.

# CHRONICLE OF THE

In this very same year <note>1654</note>, the inhabitants of the Valleys <note>the alpine valleys of Piedmont</note> were forced to endure great inconvenience and heavy burdens caused by the quartered French troops.

Thus, by God’s grace, we have now brought the **Waldensian Chronicle** up to the year 1655.

It is true that many other matters could have been added here, and those that have been recounted could have been expanded upon much more extensively; however, since we intended only to provide a brief overview of everything, and as many affairs of the Waldensians are described at length in the **Great Book of Martyrs** <note>original: *Martel-boeck*; referring to the *Martyrs Mirror*, a famous record of Christian martyrs</note>, we shall let the matter rest here.

Without any doubt, much more transpired between the year 1642 and the year 1655; but because we have chosen to record only those things we could verify, the kind reader must—until something more might follow—be satisfied with this.

It now remains for us to treat more specifically of several **blood-witnesses of Christ** <term>Bloetgetuygen Christi; a literal translation of the Greek 'martys', referring to those who testify to their faith with their lives</term> who were found among these pious people, and likewise, especially, to discuss the modern-day, horrible persecution <note>This refers to the "Piedmontese Easter" of 1655, a state-led massacre of the Waldensians</note>.
