# THE VI. CHAPTER.

## Concerning several Martyrs, and the noteworthy events that occurred regarding them.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring leafy ornamentation.</image-desc>

Kind Christian Reader, although this very brief description of what took place regarding the pious Waldensians and Reformed believers in the Piedmontese Valleys <note>The alpine regions between modern-day France and Italy where the Waldensian community sought refuge</note> at various times and in various places may and should be called nothing other than a small Book of Martyrs: yet, since they were not all martyred in one and the same way—some suffering more and others less—and because some, through God’s gracious assistance, demonstrated their great steadfastness in a truly miraculous manner; we wish to record here, for the comfort and imitation of the Saints, the steadfastness of several of the aforementioned Waldensian martyrs.

In the year 1478, the Archbishop of Embrun <note>original: "Ambron"; a city in the Hautes-Alpes which was a center of persecution against the Waldensians</note> summoned before him the two mayors of Freissinières <note>original: "Fraissiniere"</note>—namely Michiel Ruffi and Joan Girand—whom we mentioned above on page eight. They, in turn, gave as their answer: that they had nothing to do with the Archbishop, but that their case belonged before the King <note>Referring to the King of France, Louis XI, who had previously offered some protections to the inhabitants of the valleys</note>; but notwithstanding this, the Bishop—

He took these in his hands and spoke: "Just as little as I shall be able to eat these stones, so little shall you be able to root out the Religion for which I must suffer this death." Whereupon he ended his life with great steadfastness.

### WALDENSIANS.

For the *Inquisitor Monk* <note>Likely referring to a specific Catholic official tasked with investigating heresy</note> used to say that it is very dangerous to let people hear such *Waldensians* speak of their faith (as they have, in order to prove it, very powerful arguments from *Holy Scripture*); it was to be feared that those who hear them preach and teach would become much more zealous than the *Waldensians* themselves. This history is described at length in the *Book of Martyrs* <note>Likely Jean Crespin’s "Livre des Martyrs," a famous 16th-century Protestant collection</note> under the year 1536.

*In the year 1555*, when two church ministers who had come from *Geneva* to the Valleys <note>The alpine valleys of Piedmont, the traditional home of the Waldensian community</note> had undertaken a journey to *Geneva* to fetch their belongings from there, they were captured on the return journey, along with three other young men, and taken to *Chambéry*: where all five of them—after a long imprisonment, a steadfast confession of their faith, and a glorious victory against all temptations of the seductive world—received the blessed crown of martyrs for the sake of the truth. Their history is also included at length in the great *Book of Martyrs*, at the beginning of the *VI.* Book.

So also is the history of *Bartholomew Hector* very memorable; he was a bookseller who, while he had brought some books from *Geneva* into the Valleys, was seized in the Valley of *St. Martin* by certain noblemen and taken from there to *Pinerolo*, and afterwards to *Turin*: where he gave such a thorough and steadfast [confession] of his faith...

# WALDENSIANS.

For the Inquisitor Monks used to say that it is very perilous for the people to hear such Waldensians speak of their faith (because they have, to prove it, very powerful arguments from the **Holy Scripture**) fearing that those who hear them preach and teach would become even more zealous than the Waldensians themselves. ### THE SEVENTH CHAPTER.

A true and thorough account of what occurred in the persecution and bloodbath of the past year, 1655, in the **Reformed Churches** of **Piedmont**; with the addition of a refutation of the denials through which the enemies of the truth seek to make this history hated: all faithfully translated from the French language.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' containing a vase with flowers within a decorative border.</image-desc>

**T**he horrific persecution that recently befell the Reformed <term>Gereformeerde; here referring specifically to the Waldensian communities who had aligned with the Protestant Reformation</term> Churches of the **Piedmontese Valleys** has so astonished all those who have heard this sorrowful news that no person—unless they had cast off or forsaken all humanity and compassion—could hear it without terror. There will also be few found who are not eager to know the cause of such unheard-of and entirely barbaric proceedings.

And this is also the reason that moved me to publish the true account of what occurred in the aforementioned persecution; namely, that which I was able to <note>The Dutch text ends on a catchword "kon-", which would complete as "konnen vernemen" or "konnen verkrijgen" (was able to learn/obtain)</note>...

been able to learn: in order to prevent any doubtful impressions that might have arisen—or might yet arise—in anyone who may not have thoroughly understood this matter.

And it is also for this reason all the more necessary and just that I put the innocence of the persecuted on display and testify to it, because the adversaries have presumed to spread all kinds of false accusations, as if these people were **Rebels** and therefore the cause of their own misfortune.

But when the benevolent reader is pleased to take the trouble to read this short instruction impartially and without prejudice, he will easily be able to judge which party is in the right, and with what great injustice innocent people can be burdened in such circumstances.

If, in the whole world, any churches can be found that have experienced the miraculous goodness of **God** in the preservation and maintenance of his faithful members—against whom **Satan** has employed all his malice, cunning, violence, and cruelty to suppress them—then I may say with well-founded truth that the **Reformed Piedmontese Churches** <note>original: "Gereformeerde Piemontsche Kercken"</note> have always perceived this very thing in a most miraculous way.

### Chronicle of the

The Lord, who reigns in the midst of His enemies, has willed to testify to His great power, from many years past until now, in their weakness <gloss>+</gloss>.

He has maintained them through a special miracle of His power throughout all Italy; He has not allowed this glowing wick to be extinguished in the darkness of errors and unbelief; He has not permitted the light of His truth, from the times of the Apostles onward, to be placed entirely under a bushel <note>original: "Koren-mate"; a biblical reference to Matthew 5:15</note> even in this little Goshen <note>original: "Gosan"; referring to the land of Goshen where the Israelites were protected while Egypt was in darkness</note>, as these same churches thankfully acknowledge.

**Petrus Robert Olivetan** <note>Pierre Robert Olivétan (c. 1506–1538), a French scholar and cousin of John Calvin who produced the first French Protestant translation of the Bible</note>, a very learned and pious man, says in the preface of the **French Bible**, which they had printed at their own expense in **Neuchâtel** <note>original: "Nieuwenborgh"</note> in the year **1535**, concerning these poor people: *“They have always enjoyed the heavenly treasure of truth contained in the Holy Scriptures, from the time they were gifted with it by the Apostles or other messengers of Jesus Christ our Savior.”*

And that is the Truth which they have always endeavored to preserve with the highest diligence in its purity, against the many errors with which the false churches desired to corrupt it.

In this matter, their zeal was especially [aided by] **Claudius, Archbishop of Turin**, and likewise those valleys belonging to this Archbishopric during the time of the Emperor **Charlemagne** <note>original: "Carel de Groote"; Claudius of Turin (died c. 827) was famous for his opposition to the worship of images and was often cited by later Protestants as a precursor to the Reformation</note>.

Thus, they all likewise testified that the origin of their Religion did not come from **Waldo** <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140–1205), the merchant from Lyon traditionally credited with founding the Waldensians, though they often claimed an earlier apostolic origin</note>, but had come from Christ; which they also made known in their writing to the Bohemian King **Ladislaus** <note>likely referring to Ladislaus the Posthumous (1440–1457), who ruled Bohemia and Hungary</note>, stating that they therefore wished to be called not Waldensians, but Christians.

And he says further: that the Valley of **Angrogna** <note>A key valley in the Piedmont region of Italy, historically the spiritual center of the Waldensians</note> has had heretics at all times.

Everything that naturally moves a person to pity and mercy could not restrain or prevent these godless ruffians <note>original: "rabauwen"; a term for violent, lawless scoundrels or mercenaries.</note>—creatures surrendered to wickedness—from their inhuman and more than beastly raging and raving. There the good **husband** lost his faithful **wife**, the loving **mother** her tender **infant**, one **brother** the other, one **friend** the other; and all together were cast into the utmost sorrow and misery.

Some, because they lingered a little while to take some of their belongings with them, were terribly murdered. Others, being entirely defeated and terrified, remained upon the high mountains and hid themselves in the caves of the stone cliffs. There, in the snow—without fire, without food, drink, or any necessity—they were forced to remain. Among these were the elderly, the sick, pregnant women, and infants. Many of these pregnant women were so badly injured <note>Likely referring to physical trauma from the assault or the arduous escape through the mountains.</note> that they, along with the fruit of their womb, died—after having only just refreshed themselves by putting a little snow in their mouths.

### Extract from the Grants.

*In the Grant of April 9th, Year 1603, in the 3rd and 4th Articles, upon their humble petition, it is stated:*

That all inhabitants of the <term>Valleys</term> <note>Specifically the three Waldensian valleys: Pellice, Chisone, and San Martino in the Piedmont region.</note> who adhere to the <term>Reformed Religion</term> <note>The Waldensians, who by this time had formally aligned themselves with the Protestant Reformation.</note> might return home and reside in their houses, enjoy freedom of conscience, and practice their public worship in the usual and ordained places; they have received this answer from <term>His Illustrious Highness</term> <note>Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy (1562–1630). While the Dutch text uses the feminine "Hare" to match the gender of the noun "Highness," it refers to the male Duke.</note>: Regarding those in the three Valleys, they are permitted to return to their homes once again.

*And in that of the 29th of the <term>Autumn-month</term> <note>original: "Herfst-maendt," meaning September.</note>, Year 1603, in the first Article.*

Upon the humble petition of the Reformed, who once again desired the same things they had previously requested for all places and communities of the aforementioned Valleys, His Illustrious Highness has made it known: that all those of the Religion who have departed from their houses and dwellings in the mentioned three Valleys may return home and may live in all three Valleys, without exception of any place.

### Chronicle of the...

And under the Seal, this very same point is repeated: The intention of **Her Royal Highness** <note>Christine of France, acting as Regent.</note> is not that the **Liberties** and rights shared with the **Petitioners** by His Serene Highness Lord **Charles Emmanuel** <note>Charles Emmanuel I (1562–1630).</note> in the year 1620 should be diminished or increased, these remaining herewith in their full force.

From this it clearly appears that the pretext for this persecution—which was also pointed out to **Gastaldo** <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the judge and auditor who issued the infamous 1655 edict ordering the Waldensians to leave their homes or convert to Catholicism.</note> at the start of it—claiming that the **Reformed** had overstepped their designated boundaries, is entirely untrue; and that the **Reformed** driven by him from their houses and their goods were not located outside the circle of their permitted residences.

Therefore, the opposing parties—since they can easily see the emptiness of this first pretext and fear that, if the matter were thoroughly investigated, **Her Royal Highness** would not fail to protect the **Reformed** in the just **Liberties** they possess—do not want to allow **Her Royal Highness** to be correctly informed of the case. Instead, to make the **Reformed** more hated by Her Highness and to embitter her all the more against them, they have brought forth all kinds of shameful and blatant lies and false accusations against them.

I. The <note>Original Dutch catchword: "I. Het"</note>

<meta>This page continues the legal and religious defense of the Waldensian communities (the Reformed Churches of the Valleys). # Chronicle of the

Reformed Churches in the Valleys <note>The "Valleys" (Dalen) refers to the Alpine ancestral lands of the Waldensians in the Piedmont region, situated between modern-day France and Italy.</note>, which have existed from time immemorial—namely, that in times of need, they have gathered together in a Synod <note>original: "Synodus" – a formal assembly of church elders and ministers to decide on doctrine and governance.</note> to deliberate on all matters concerning their congregations—have not wished to change this practice. The Roman Catholics do exactly the same; for example, when a Diocese <note>original: "Bisdom"</note> is situated partly in one Sovereign’s territory and partly in another’s. Therefore, the Reformed cannot be accused regarding this matter except in an improper way; for in this, they have also not acted against the honor and due obedience owed to their High Authority <note>original: "Overigheydt" – referring here to the Duke of Savoy, their sovereign ruler.</note>.

Finally, the Reformed churches have been falsely accused of seeking help and protection from foreign Princes, Lords, and Estates <note>original: "Standen" – the representative political bodies of other nations, such as the Dutch Republic or Swiss Cantons.</note>. In this, they have again been treated with violence and injustice; for it is certain—as the aforementioned Princes and Estates are willing and ready to testify—that they have received no writings, nor even the smallest scrap of paper <note>original: "cedeltjen" – a diminutive term for a note or slip, emphasizing that there was absolutely no communication.</note>, from these churches.

But as for the fact that the well-regarded Princes have sent letters to His Royal Highness <note>The Duke of Savoy.</note>; these were based on nothing other than pure religious zeal and arose from a heartfelt compassion for their oppressed co-religionists <note>original: "Geloofs-genooten" – literally "faith-associates" or brothers in faith.</note>.

So likewise have the Estates,

### WALDENSIANS.

...from the oppressed Valley-folk <note>original: "Dael-luijden" – the inhabitants of the Piedmontese valleys.</note>, but from other places, news was received of how horribly their dear fellow members have been treated; how many thousands of them—in the coldest of winter, with women and children, small and great, healthy and sick, and that without any prior presentation or hearing of their legal grounds and ancestral residency rights, and without the acceptance of any **Protest**, **Appeal**, or humble pleas—have had to leave their houses and property within three days, upon pain of death.

It was no less known to the Estates <note>The "Estates" (Standen) refers to the governing bodies of Protestant nations, such as the Dutch Republic, who were observing these events.</note> that these poor oppressed people were cut off from all access to His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy (1634–1675).</note>, their natural and most gracious Prince and Lord: and that the Council <term>for the propagation of the Faith and the extirpation of Heretics</term> <note>original: "de propaganda Fide, & extirpandis Hæreticis" – a Catholic administrative body established to spread Catholicism and eliminate Protestantism, which the Waldensians viewed as a "heresy-hunting" tribunal.</note>, which is ordained for the spreading of the Faith and the rooting out of Heretics, has presumed to speak in this matter against all right and equity. Therefore, they [the Estates] believed it not unseemly that they should kindly persist and request of His Royal Highness on our behalf, as for their poor oppressed brothers, that he would be pleased to take the matter of his faithful Subjects—those belonging to the **Reformed Religion**—into his own hands, and to restore them to their rights; that he would not allow them to be oppressed by their adversaries through improper coercion, as has already occurred.

# CHRONICLE OF THE

And since the aforementioned Council <term>the Council for the Propagation of the Faith</term> <note>As noted on the previous page, this was the Catholic body coordinating the persecution of the Reformed Waldensians.</note> has now taken it upon itself to exercise authority over the Reformed, and has undoubtedly given the order to carry out its intended resolution and purpose through force of arms—just as the same has already occurred, alas! through all kinds of more-than-Barbaric cruelties: and that the poor oppressed people were finally forced to protect themselves against such unjust violence and inhuman tyranny, the likes of which have never been heard in any history; so it is to be hoped that everyone who views and considers the aforementioned without prejudice and with true impartiality will have to acknowledge that they have not [risen up] against His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy (1634–1675).</note>, their natural Prince and Lord—to whose service they are not only willing and prepared to pledge their bodies and lives, their houses and goods, but also for whom and for whose entire Royal House they heartily and fervently pray to the good God for lasting peace, salvation, and welfare—but much more against an unruly multitude of Bandits, Robbers, and **Murderers** <note>original: "Moonaers" — likely a variant or transcription error for *moordenaars* (murderers).</note>, who, in the hope that the inhabitants and the **Valleys** would be given to them as plunder, have flocked there in great numbers, destroying everything with fire and sword: also against the improper violence of the aforementioned Council, and especially against the **Marquis of Pianezza** <note>The Marquis of Pianezza (1612–1675) was the commander of the ducal troops who led the "Piedmontese Easter" massacre of 1655.</note>, who, despite the given Princely word, attacked them unawares, they having been able to obtain no hearing from their regular authorities...

->## WALDENSIANS.<-

<meta>The text continues from the previous page's description of the Waldensians being blocked from reaching their sovereign.</meta>

...to come / before His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II (1634–1675), Duke of Savoy.</note> / their most gracious Prince / to whom they / after God / have their only refuge / seeking their comfort from him alone / expecting their help and deliverance from him alone / [but with] all access blocked / they are forced to take up arms. The promises that the Marquis of Pianezza <note>The commander of the Savoyard troops who led the 1655 massacre known as the Piedmontese Easter.</note> makes here, and thereafter repeats in a specially established Treaty with some individuals from Bobbio and Villar <note>Bobbio Pellice and Villar Pellice, Waldensian settlements in the Piedmontese valleys.</note>, have not been confirmed by Her Royal Highness <note>Christina of France, the Dowager Duchess and Regent of Savoy.</note>, as he himself has admitted, because they did not wish to apostatize <note>original: "afvallen"; meaning to renounce their Protestant faith for Roman Catholicism.</note>: for the rest would not have prevented them from being taken into the protection of Her Royal Highness, since the Marquis extended certain protection to all those who would apostatize, even if it were but a single person. This point cannot in any way be invalidated by the Marquis's excuse; for he says that this is a mercy which the Prince was able to grant to those who swore off the Reformed Religion: and that by this renunciation, the alleged Rebellion <term>Rebellion|The Savoyard authorities legally defined the Waldensians' refusal to relocate from their ancestral lands as an act of "rebellye" or treason against the sovereign.</term> of living outside the designated places ceased and was no longer taken into consideration.

# W A L D E N S E N.

For his claim that they deserved the punishment because they took up arms and went to the aid of the inhabitants of the Valley of Lucerna <note>The Val Pellice, known then as the Valley of Lucerna, was a center of Waldensian life.</note> has no foundation whatsoever; it is clear that this is merely a vain invention to carry out their bloody intent with some appearance of legality. For—to say nothing for now of what will follow—when the Reformed <note>The Waldensians, a group that predated the Reformation but eventually aligned with the Protestant movement.</note> attempted to protect their lives and those of their wives and children against the gruesome murderers by whom they were treacherously attacked, they did nothing other than what is right and just; for it is natural for anyone to defend themselves against such cruelty whenever possible. If some individuals from the Valleys of Saint Martin and Perosa <note>Val San Martino and Val Perosa, neighboring Alpine valleys where Waldensian communities lived.</note> were found among their brothers during that miserable time, these were only a few private individuals—perhaps barely one in a hundred. Should the innocent as well as the guilty therefore have to endure the punishment for this alleged rebellion? For only those caught in the act, and those who could be proven to have taken up arms, should have been banished.

I do not wish now to speak of the question of whether, and under what circumstances, it is permitted for subjects <term>Onderdanen</term> to protect their liberties—and especially the freedom of conscience <term>vryheydt der Conscientie</term>—by force of arms when those who are placed over them seek to oppress them through unlawful violence. Since this matter has been dealt with by various learned men, not only in former times but also in our own, it is not necessary to speak of it here.

For it is well known that the *Reformed Valley-folk* <term>Gereformeerde Dael-luyden</term> <note>The Waldensians living in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont.</note>—even though they were all driven from their houses and property without any cause by the *Edict* <term>Edict</term> that *Gastaldo* <note>Andrea Gastaldo, the Auditor of the Duke of Savoy, who issued the decree of January 25, 1655, ordering the Waldensians to relocate or convert to Catholicism within three days.</note> issued in the bitterest of the cold winter, on pain of death—sent many deputies and *Petitions* <term>Supplicatien</term> to His Royal Highness <note>Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy.</note>. They did this so that their legal grounds might be heard, and so that they might be maintained and protected in their properties, which they had inherited by virtue of ancient grants <note>Refers to the historic treaties, such as the 1561 Treaty of Cavour, which granted the Waldensians limited religious freedom.</note>. 

They persisted in this humble and submissive appeal without ceasing, right up until the day they were attacked by the *Army*. Yet, the *Council for the Propagation of the Faith* <term>Raedt de propaganda Fide</term> <note>The "Congregatio de Propaganda Fide," a body of the Catholic Church tasked with missionary work and, in this context, the eradication of Protestantism in Savoy.</note> never wished to allow them a hearing before His Royal Highness. Thus, this matter was not judged before the Prince's Council, but rather by the aforementioned *Assembly for the Propagation of the Faith*.

# C O P Y ,

## Of the confirmation of the obtained liberty and Agreement, established in the year 1654.

**We Charles Emmanuel, *by the grace of God Duke of Savoy, Prince of Piedmont, and King of Cyprus.***

Since we—through the Agreements of June 2nd and 4th, as well as of September 29th of the year 1653—have granted and promised to the inhabitants of the Valleys of Luserna, Perosa, and San Martino, Roccapiatta, San Bartolomeo, Prarostino, and the places belonging thereto, who profess the <term>so-called Reformed Religion</term> <note>Original: "vermeynde Gereformeerde Religie." This was a standard legal phrasing used by Catholic authorities at the time to refer to Protestantism without acknowledging it as a "true" or "legal" church.</note>, to allow them from now on the very same liberties and favors which they obtained from the late Duke Charles Emmanuel and Duke Victor Amadeus, my grandfather and father of glorious memory; but which they have not been able to have recorded in the <term>Acts and State Archives</term> <note>Original: "Actis en Lants-Archiven." Official registration was the final step required for a royal decree to become enforceable law.</note> until now, by reason of the French troops who stayed in the Valleys this past winter, and because of the damage they caused in the surrounding places. Nevertheless, it is our will and intention that the same [liberties] shall be enjoyed from this time forward, without any hindrance, until they are recorded within these following three months.

# Front Cover of the Manuscript

This manuscript is bound in a classic **half-leather** <term>A binding technique where leather covers the spine and corners for durability, while the rest of the cover is finished with less expensive decorative paper.</term> style. The central portion of the cover is decorated with **marbled paper** <note>Created by floating pigments on a liquid surface and transferring the pattern to paper, marbling was a popular way to make books both attractive and unique.</note> featuring a "stone" or "shell" design. This organic, irregular pattern displays a palette of olive green, terracotta brown, and cream.

The dark brown leather of the spine is decorated with sets of horizontal **blind-tooled** <term>Decorative impressions pressed into leather using heated tools without applying gold leaf or color.</term> lines. On the outer edge of the cover, a thin metal guard or clasp component remains, which served to protect the edges of the pages and keep the volume tightly closed when not in use.

<summary>This page describes the physical front cover of the manuscript, which features a durable half-leather binding and decorative stone-patterned marbled paper.</summary>
<keywords>bookbinding, half-leather, marbled paper, blind-tooling, manuscript exterior, preservation</keywords>
